name: Net Present Value (NPV)
description: Calculate the net present value of a single future cash flow discounted back to today.
formula: NPV = −Initial Investment + Future Cash Flow / (1 + Discount Rate)^Years
business_contexts: an investor assessing NPV of a single future payout
a company assessing NPV of a capital project with one future cash inflow
a private equity firm assessing NPV of a planned exit
a real estate investor assessing NPV of a planned property sale
a manufacturer assessing NPV of a one-time equipment payoff
question_patterns: Given the initial investment, future cash flow, discount rate, and years below, what is the NPV?
Calculate NPV from the figures given, discounting the single future cash flow back to today.
What is the net present value of this investment, given the figures below?
Calculate NPV by discounting the future cash flow and netting out the initial investment given.
Using the figures below, what is the NPV?
solution_logic: Step 1: Calculate the discount factor = (1 + discount_rate)^years
Step 2: Calculate present value of future cash flow = future_cash_flow / discount factor
Step 3: Calculate NPV = present value of future cash flow − initial_investment
key_insight: NPV can legitimately come out negative — that's not an error, it means the discounted future cash flow doesn't cover the upfront investment.
common_mistakes: Forgetting to discount the future cash flow and simply subtracting the initial investment from its face value
Applying the discount rate as simple division (rate × years) instead of compounding it as (1 + rate)^years
framework_soundbite: NPV discounts the future cash flow back to today, then nets out what it cost to get there — a negative result means the deal doesn't clear the bar.
